#845. Bompastor's risks pay off as Chelsea go top of WSL

Chelsea efficient Man City with first loss of the season

In any big encounter you will often hear managers say it is the "fine margins" that decide a game of football.

Sometimes it is luck. Sometimes it is individual brilliance. But on Saturday it was Sonia Bompastor's bold decisions that helped Chelsea beat Manchester City 1-0.

The top-of-the-table Women's Super League clash was as intriguing as you would hope it to be and both managers needed to be on their toes.

Chelsea boss Bompastor "took responsibility" and brought off struggling defender Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes in, and it had the desired effect.

City striker Khadija Shaw was not able to get in behind like she had done in the early stages, and Buchanan's replacement Veerle Buurman shone.

Was it a tactical substitution or was Buchanan injured?

When the fourth official's board went up showing the number of the player Buurman would replace, there was confusion from Chelsea players.

It was clearly not planned, nor had Buchanan asked to come off. There was no apparent injury as she jogged off and she was clearly upset, heading straight down the tunnel.

Asked to clarify the situation, Bompastor said: "Yesterday in training she got a knock to her head in contact with a team-mate but she was fine.

"She was fine in the evening and we assessed her again this morning and everything was fine. I had that information before the game.

"But I felt from watching her at the beginning of the game that she was not herself. I took the responsibility to make the substitution.

"I felt I was almost forced to do that. I know my player and she was not in the game."

Whether Buchanan's shaky start was down to that knock is unclear, but Bompastor knew her decision was a risk and was willing to act immediately.

Buurman instantly marshalled Shaw, and City's early threat was quietened as Chelsea regained control and ended the half a goal up thanks to Sandy Baltimore.

Shaw did not record a shot on target and in-form England international Lauren Hemp was quiet as Buurman performed well in a stubborn Chelsea backline.

City manager Andree Jeglertz said he did not think the switch "changed the picture", but he was outsmarted by Bompastor during the 90 minutes.

Bompastor admitted she had not spoken properly with Buchanan at full-time but promised to "explain myself to her".

"I just told her a few words. My assistant coach Camille Abily will have done that already probably and I think everything will be fine," said the Frenchwoman.

"I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I'm always direct and honest so they have the information. It won't be any different."

The risky substitution was compounded by an injury to striker Melvine Malard 23 minutes later, meaning Chelsea's XI was tweaked twice before half-time.

Not normally one to bring on players at the break, Bompastor was smart and hooked goalscorer Baltimore, who was likely still buzzing from her impact.

She was replaced by Maika Hamano, who went on to play the ball through to Alyssa Thompson when she was brought down by City goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita, and she was shown a straight red card as a result, ending the visitors' comeback hopes.

"We knew going into the second half we only had one substitution slot and we knew Sandy has been playing lots of minutes," said Bompastor.

"I knew she probably didn't have the legs to go more than maybe 60 minutes and I knew I didn't have more slots after that. I was forced into this one as well.

"It paid off and that's good. Sandy was doing well but she knows the reason why we made that decision.

"That's the first time I experienced that kind of substitution in the first half. It's good for my own experience."

Bompastor's bravery was rewarded and, while City certainly had their chances, Chelsea defended resiliently to see out the narrow win.

Jeglertz could not find a solution to Chelsea's attacking threats, which came largely from wide areas via Ellie Carpenter and Thompson.

Vivianne Miedema returned from injury and looked sharp when she came on for City in the second half, but it was not enough to change the result.

In contrast, Bompastor's risks proved the difference, and they were made with former Chelsea boss Emma Hayes, who mastered the art of bullish decisions, watching on in the stands alongside Sarina Wiegman at Stamford Bridge.

Chelsea's victory bumped them back up to the WSL summit, a point above City, while Buurman picked up the player-of-the-match award.

"It paid off today. You have to be brave to make that decision in that moment because you know bringing in a player in the game is a risk," said Bompastor.

"We had a good conversation with Veerle and she was clear on why she wasn't starting the game. That clarity was important for when she came in.

"She had a really good performance against a top player. Sometimes when it doesn't work, it's not so positive, but today it was.

"You have to react and be the one that analyses the situation and make decisions. I'm used to it, even if you don't see lots of substitutions in the first half most of the time in football."

#843. A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer

For some breast cancer survivors, the effects of treatment can linger long after their cancer care ends. Memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and persistent exhaustion can interfere with everyday life, sometimes for years. Now, researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have found promising early evidence that a supplement containing a naturally occurring molecule could help relieve these symptoms.

The molecule, called oxaloacetate, is already present in the human body and plays an important role in how cells generate energy. In a small clinical trial, breast cancer survivors who took the supplement for eight weeks reported noticeable improvements in thinking, memory, concentration, and fatigue.

The results, published in JCO Oncology Advances, also showed improvements on cognitive tests measuring how quickly participants processed information and performed tasks requiring planning, attention, and mental flexibility. Although larger studies are needed to confirm the findings, the results suggest a potentially new way to address a problem that has long been difficult to treat.

"Cancer-related cognitive impairment can persist long after treatment ends and can have a significant impact on a person's daily life, yet we still have very few effective treatments for it," said Dr. Patricia Ganz, the study's first author and a distinguished professor of medicine at UCLA's David Geffen School of Medicine and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

Why Brain Fog Can Persist After Cancer Treatment

Cognitive difficulties are a lasting concern for many people who survive breast cancer. Researchers estimate that roughly 15% to 25% experience ongoing problems with memory, concentration, or other thinking abilities after their diagnosis and treatment. These symptoms are often described as "chemo brain" or "brain fog."

Despite the name, chemotherapy is not necessarily the only cause. Scientists increasingly recognize that cancer-related cognitive impairment can develop through several overlapping processes. The cancer itself, chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, inflammation, hormonal changes, and other biological and behavioral influences may all contribute.

Because the causes are complicated and effective treatments remain limited, researchers are investigating ways to address the underlying changes that may disrupt normal brain function.

One area of interest involves the relationship between inflammation, brain chemistry, and energy production. Inflammation linked to cancer and its treatments may interfere with glutamate signaling, an important part of communication between nerve cells. It may also disturb the processes that allow brain cells to produce and use energy efficiently. Together, these disruptions could contribute to difficulties with thinking and persistent mental exhaustion.

Oxaloacetate attracted the UCLA team's attention because it participates in both cellular energy production and the regulation of glutamate. The researchers wanted to learn whether providing additional oxaloacetate through a supplement might reduce the cognitive symptoms and fatigue experienced by cancer survivors.

Testing Oxaloacetate for Brain Fog and Fatigue

To investigate, the researchers carried out a phase II clinical trial involving 18 women who had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer between one and five years earlier. All participants were experiencing substantial cognitive difficulties when they entered the study.

The women were approximately 50 years old on average. Most had undergone chemotherapy, and nearly 90% were still receiving endocrine therapy during the trial.

Each participant was instructed to take 500 milligrams of oxaloacetate twice a day for eight weeks. The researchers tracked changes in cognitive symptoms using questionnaires completed by the participants, along with standardized tests designed to evaluate memory, attention, processing speed, and executive function. Executive function includes the mental abilities needed to organize activities, maintain focus, make plans, and manage tasks.

The study also examined fatigue, sleep, anxiety, depression, physical health, and mental well-being. Throughout the treatment period, the team monitored participants for possible side effects.

Brain Fog Scores Improved After Eight Weeks

Of the 18 women enrolled, 16 completed the full eight weeks of supplementation. Every participant who finished the treatment reported significant improvement in her cognitive symptoms.

The changes were particularly striking on the study's main measure of perceived cognitive impairment. Before treatment, the participants had an average score of 29.1. After eight weeks, that average had climbed to 55.5, placing the group in the range considered normal rather than impaired.

Signs of improvement were already apparent after four weeks, and the benefits reported by participants generally became more pronounced as treatment continued.

The results extended beyond memory and concentration. Participants reported significantly less fatigue, including the mental exhaustion that can make everyday activities difficult. They also described meaningful improvements in their ability to function physically.

Standardized cognitive testing provided additional encouraging evidence. Researchers observed improvements in processing speed and executive function, suggesting that some aspects of thinking performance may have improved alongside the participants' perceptions of their symptoms.

However, the scientists emphasized that these results remain preliminary because the trial included so few participants.

Promising Results, but More Research Is Needed

Oxaloacetate was generally well tolerated during the eight-week study. The most frequently reported side effects involved the digestive system, including indigestion, bloating, constipation, diarrhea, and nausea.

Two women stopped taking the supplement because of gastrointestinal symptoms. No serious adverse events were recorded.

Despite the encouraging improvements, the researchers cautioned against drawing firm conclusions about the supplement's effectiveness. The trial was small and did not include a placebo group or another comparison group. Without that comparison, it is not possible to determine whether oxaloacetate itself caused the improvements.

"These early findings give us a strong reason to continue studying oxaloacetate as a potential approach for managing cognitive problems after breast cancer treatment," Ganz said.

Larger Clinical Trial Will Test the Supplement's Benefits

To build on these initial findings, the UCLA team has been preparing a randomized, placebo-controlled phase II clinical trial involving breast cancer survivors with cancer-related cognitive impairment. The study was expected to begin enrolling participants in late 2026.

By comparing oxaloacetate with a placebo, the researchers hope to establish whether the supplement produces measurable benefits beyond those that might occur without active treatment.

The investigators are also conducting preclinical research in mice to better understand how oxaloacetate affects the body and brain. These experiments include a placebo-controlled study examining whether the molecule produces similar improvements (improved fatigue and physical function) in animals.

The research received partial financial support from the Breast Cancer Research Foundation and the National Cancer Institute.

In addition to Ganz, the study's authors were Kathleen Van Dyk, PhD, Catherine M. Crespi, PhD, Laura Petersen, MS, Mina Sedrak, MD, MS, and Julienne Bower, PhD, all affiliated with UCLA.

#841. 'No racism in Spain' – De la Fuente message for Tuchel

Luis de la Fuente agreed a contract extension in September to stay as Spain boss until 2032

Luis de la Fuente has dismissed concerns over racism in Spanish football before the national team's Uefa Nations League meeting with England in Madrid on Sunday.

Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel had earlier confirmed he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture, which will determine who finishes top of League A Group 3.

While he has stressed he didn't expect there to be any incidents, the visit will be England's first to the Spanish capital since a notorious 2004 encounter at the Bernabeu was overshadowed by racist chanting directed at their players.

Spain head coach De la Fuente was asked whether Tuchel's message to his players showed there was still work needed to tackle racism in Spain.

But he responded: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.

"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."

The Spanish Football Federation was fined last month and ordered to partially close a stadium after supporters directed Islamophobic and xenophobic chants towards Muslims during a match against Egypt in Barcelona.

In the domestic game, Real Madrid's Brazilian forward Vinicius Jr has been a vocal anti-racism campaigner after frequently being on the end of racist chanting - and worse. In 2024 three Valencia fans were sentenced to eight months in prison for abusing him at a match.

Uefa operates a three-step protocol, allowing referees to stop matches, take players off the pitch temporarily and, ultimately, abandon a game if discriminatory behaviour continues.

Tuchel said on Friday: "Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid]. And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch."

However, when asked again about his views at a pre-match news conference on Saturday, Tuchel added: "I never talk about racism in Spain.

"I answered politely a question about what happens, I never expect racism. I got asked, 'what will happen if and if and if?'. And I said, 'if it happens, there's a protocol in place'. That's it.

"But my trust is that we have a friendly atmosphere, that we have an atmosphere who is clearly in favour of the Spanish team, and that football does what it does best: brings people together and not divide people."

Midfielder Declan Rice said: "In the past, I've experienced that in Montenegro and Bulgaria and there was a protocol in place that we followed - we came off the pitch. We know exactly where we are as a group on that.

"The times we are in now, 2026, there should never be racism in football. It's shocking we still have it in the game today.

"I don't want to think about if one of our players or their players is racially abused because that would be a horrible mark on football."

Focusing on the match itself, De la Fuente believed both teams are currently at the pinnacle of world football, although he rejected the suggestion one could simply replicate the other's playing style.

Spain were crowned World Cup winners in the summer, while England finished third after losing to Argentina in the semi-finals.

"I prefer the Spanish model. It's very recognisable, the players are perfectly adapted," said De la Fuente. "The English model is very good, but you have to have that type of player. Neither England can play like Spain, nor Spain like England."

He suggested Spain had faced increasingly aggressive opposition as their recent success had raised expectations.

"It's our best moment in a long time," added De la Fuente, whose side also lifted the Euro 2024 title by beating England. "They are all much more aggressive to beat us now than in other times."

He also defended the value of Spanish players, arguing their performances often outweighed their transfer-market prices compared with those in the Premier League.

"Spanish footballers surprise me that, compared to what is paid in England, they are very cheap," he explained. "I see them as better, in my opinion. Everyone in their market can set the prices."

On the fitness of forward Lamine Yamal, he remained cautious over whether the Barcelona teenager would start or how long he could manage.

"We will see if he is a starter, but if he comes out, it's because he's fit to play," said De la Fuente.

#839. An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin

A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected new approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that rapamycin, a medication also studied for its effects on aging, can improve blood flow in the brains of middle-aged adults who carry a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's.

The findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear. The research also adds to the University of Missouri's growing contributions to understanding and potentially preventing the most common form of dementia.

The study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building. Her work focuses on identifying changes in the brain that occur before Alzheimer's symptoms develop and finding ways to intervene early.

Why Brain Blood Flow Matters for Alzheimer's Risk

A major focus of Lin's research is the APOE4 gene variant, which is associated with a substantially increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease later in life.

People who carry APOE4 can experience reduced blood flow in certain areas of the brain years before they begin having noticeable memory difficulties. Because these circulation changes can occur so early, researchers believe they could provide an important warning sign of increased Alzheimer's risk.

Lin's latest findings suggest that improving brain circulation with an existing medication may be one way to address these early changes.

"Alzheimer's tends to happen more in older people, especially for those with APOE4," Lin said. "If we can slow down aging in the brain for those people most at risk, maybe we can reduce the risk of them developing Alzheimer's disease."

Rapamycin is already used in medicine to prevent the immune system from rejecting transplanted organs and to treat certain rare conditions. However, researchers have also been investigating its potential to slow biological aging and protect the brain.

Before joining the University of Missouri, Lin conducted experiments involving mice that carried APOE4. Her earlier research showed that rapamycin could slow brain aging and increase blood flow in these animals.

Those results prompted an important question: Could rapamycin produce similar benefits in people who have a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer's but have not yet developed the disease?

To investigate, Lin studied healthy adults between the ages of 45 and 65, including people who carried APOE4 and others who did not.

All participants received a low daily dose of rapamycin for four weeks. When researchers examined the results, they found a notable difference between the two groups.

Brain blood flow improved among participants carrying APOE4, but the same benefit was not observed in those without the gene variant. This suggests that rapamycin may have particular potential for people whose genetics place them at greater risk of Alzheimer's.

Although the study did not establish whether the treatment could prevent Alzheimer's or preserve memory over time, the improved circulation offers a promising direction for future research.

Women With the Alzheimer's Risk Gene Saw the Greatest Benefits

Another intriguing finding emerged when the researchers examined differences between male and female participants.

Women carrying APOE4 experienced the largest improvements in brain blood flow following treatment. That result may be especially important because women account for nearly two-thirds of people living with Alzheimer's disease.

"We also found that females with APOE4 saw the greatest improvement in brain blood flow, which is significant given that nearly two-thirds of people with Alzheimer's are women," she said. "This research is an example of precision medicine, as we work to identify who can benefit from this drug the most."

The results highlight the potential of precision medicine, an approach that considers individual characteristics, including genetics, when determining which treatments may be most effective.

Rather than assuming that a medication will benefit everyone equally, researchers hope to identify the people most likely to respond.

Moving Alzheimer's Discoveries Toward Human Treatments

Lin, who is also a professor in the university's College of Arts and Science, credits Mizzou's collaborative research environment with helping advance discoveries like these.

At the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building, scientists and medical professionals work together in the same facility. This collaboration is designed to help move promising laboratory findings into human clinical studies more quickly.

The latest results provide an encouraging starting point for investigating whether rapamycin could eventually help delay or reduce Alzheimer's risk in genetically vulnerable individuals. More research will be needed to determine whether the changes in brain blood flow lead to lasting improvements in brain health or a lower likelihood of developing the disease.

The study, "EXPRESS: Rapamycin increases cerebral blood flow and modulates metabolic, inflammatory, and microbiome profiles in healthy middle-aged APOE4 carriers: a pilot single-arm trial" was published in Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism.

#838. De la Fuente feels the strain as Lamine Yamal club v country debate rages in Spain

Head coach hits out at ‘lies’ as suggestions of preferential treatment for young star overshadow preparations for England game in Madrid

From the London Palladium to Madrid’s Metropolitano, they’re all here. On Sunday night, the footballers who lifted the game’s biggest awards meet again three weeks later and on the field this time, dinner jackets but not a single man left behind. Harry Kane, the Ballon d’Or and Gerd Müller trophy winner. Unai Simón, holder of the Lev Yashin award. Luis de la Fuente, the coach of the year who on Thursday night announced that also joining them will be Lamine Yamal, the kid who lifted the Kopa award as the best young player for the third year running and said he would have preferred Pau Cubarsí to be standing there instead. And, yes, Cubarsí will be there too for the final Nations League group game.

At 1.45pm on Friday the world and European champions landed back at Madrid’s Barajas airport from Prague, where they had won again, before making their way by bus to their Las Rozas HQ, around the M40 motorway to the north-west of the capital. At about the same time, Lamine Yamal arrived from Barcelona, due in at midday. As was Mikel Oyarzabal, scorer of the winner at Euro 2024 and Spain’s top marksman this summer (not that he would ever tell you so) from San Sebastián. At 7.30pm, they trained, preparing to meet the World Cup semi-finalists and the team they defeated in Berlin at the end of Euro 2024. Two starters from the World Cup final will be absent: Dani Olmo and the captain, 2024 Ballon d’Or winner Rodri, are injured. But everyone else will be there.

“I’ve got good news,” De la Fuente said after a 2-0 victory over Czechia. “Lamine is in perfect condition and really looking forward to it and Mikel has just become a father; he will appreciate the chance to sleep.”

It is good news too, even if an absurd debate has dominated this international break regarding Lamine Yamal. In a country where there’s always a debate to be had even when there is none, where two clubs still come first even when the selección may again be the best ever, maybe it was inevitable. All the more so, perhaps, as Spain assimilates the idea that for the first time maybe they have the world’s best player now, with everything that brings, a single player sometimes dominating the agenda even around a team that is all about the collective. But that did not stop it infuriating De la Fuente.

It began when Lamine Yamal didn’t join the squad to prepare for the trip to Czechia, the door left open for him to return to face England in the game that really excited. Never mind that the same plan had been put into place with Oyarzabal, that during the last, four-game international break Lamine Yamal was the only player to play more than the 270-minute limit the manager had set, the accusation came that the teenager had been given preferential treatment.

There was context too, a previous disconnect between Barcelona and the federation over Lamine Yamal’s treatment and the demands made, with Hansi Flick complaining that Spain hadn’t taken care of him and De la Fuente expressing surprise at the lack of understanding from a man who had been a national team coach. Now, some claimed in columns and furious debates on television and radio, the country had given in to the club.

De la Fuente wasn’t having it, bemoaning the “sophists” out there. “The saddest, most lamentable thing there is in life is to speak without knowledge,” he said before the game in Prague. “I’m here to cast light. Lamine had some discomfort on his knee and a scan showed some liquid on his knee, so I took the decision that rather than coming here, travelling, he should rest, get treatment. I am optimistic he can join us on Friday. Is that clear?”

It was put to Spain’s coach that this was a bit unlike him, that he seemed unusually angry. “What upsets me are the lies, the things that are made up, the lack of rigour. And in the face of that, I rebel. So, maybe I said more than I would, but sometimes it is the only way to make people realise, to see. I cannot bear people who lie, who try to mislead.”

This was a public expression of something that has privately baffled De la Fuente at times. Besides, what’s the alternative? To leave Lamine Yamal and Oyarzabal out entirely? How can it be anything other than a good thing that he, that they, are available to play against England? Rather than preferential treatment, couldn’t this be interpreted as commitment, an effort to be there? How can there be a debate, how can there be any doubt, about a team in the place Spain are in?

There has never been a European champion like Spain were in Germany, winning every game and defeating four World Cup-winning countries; there may not have been a world champion as quietly superior as they were this summer either, anaesthetising France and Argentina. There has never been a team with a run like this, either, De la Fuente always keen to stress how insatiable they are, how their hunger remains intact.

Spain last lost 23 games ago – and that was on penalties against Portugal in the Nationals League final – and have not been beaten in 120 minutes for 43 matches.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Spain are a team, a federation, with a clarity of idea and identity, an environment and continuity, that underlines that success is not chance and that it goes beyond this XI and this generation. Marc Roca offers an example among many: one of five new players in the squad, he has joined the seniors for the first time aged 29 but, like so many of his teammates, he worked with De la Fuente with the under-21s.

Martín Zubimendi offers another: at the World Cup he played 21 minutes, coming on in the final to run the game; at the Euros he was introduced in the final, too. Both times, he had to replace the best midfielder on earth; both times, it had the perfect ending. With Rodri absent again, this is another opportunity for an Arsenal player reduced to barely 100 Premier League minutes. “There are players who play better here than with their clubs,” De la Fuente said.

There is a line the coach is fond of repeating. “Rodri is the best midfielder in the world; Martín is the second best,” he said. Sure, that’s bias talking, faith, but when he insists, again and again, that his players are the best in the world they do then have a habit of backing him up. If Zubimendi is not the second-best midfielder in the world, if Rodri is not the best, Fabián Ruiz holds the Champions League and the World Cup.

And what of Pedri? If Simón had not lifted the Yashin award, surely David Raya would have. Besides, De la Fuente said: “Unai Simón is not just the best goalkeeper in the world, he is the best person in the world.” If Lamine Yamal was disappointed to win the Kopa, that was because Cubarsí deserved it and he thought the Ballon d’Or might have been his, which it surely will be one year soon.

The Euros and the World Cup suggest De la Fuente may be right, the run does too, and so did their night out at the Palladium. Only one of those men clutching prizes in London isn’t his, and he’s coming to Madrid on Sunday, the Metropolitano packed for as good a game as you can get anywhere, the teenager who may yet mark an entire generation joining them, too. So welcome once more, Harry. You’re in good company again.

#837. The 'manager's dream' who has put NI one game from history

Terry Devlin scored his first Northern Ireland goal against Ukraine

It was a moment that Northern Ireland needed.

When Terry Devlin picked the ball up on the edge of the area in the 68th minute against Ukraine there was only one thought in his mind.

And when the ball flew into the corner Windsor Park erupted at another highlight of a Nations League campaign that has been a real feel-good story so far.

Heading into Saturday's game they had yet to concede a goal, but the one thing they had lacked was a home win - or even a home goal - after drawing blanks in stalemates with Hungary and Georgia in Belfast.

They had already come close when Jamie Donley slotted home in the first half but the forward had strayed offside, leaving the moment the hosts had been waiting for to come through Devlin's superb winner.

It leaves Northern Ireland's Nations League fate in their own hands, and a draw or better in Hungary would secure promotion to League A for the first time.

For Northern Ireland boss Michael O'Neill, it was a huge moment from a player who he said is "a bit of a dream" to manage.

"Terry's a great lad. He deserves everything he'll get from the game and he's one of those lads that maximises what he has," O'Neill said about the 23-year-old Portsmouth defender.

Northern Ireland beat Ukraine to move closer to Nations League promotion

Devlin nets winner as NI top Nations League group

Speaking about his versatility - Devlin can play in midfield as well as a full-back on either side - O'Neill added: "He does it with no fuss. He tries to do it to the best of his ability.

"He's a bit of a dream for a manager and he has the ability to contribute goals."

The average age of O'Neill's starting XI on Saturday was just 22.9 with eight players aged 23 or younger.

Devlin epitomises what this team are all about with his all-action display rewarded with a first international goal.

A versatile option, he broke through into senior football with his hometown club Dungannon Swifts in the Irish Premiership and impressive performances for Glentoran saw him earn a move to Portsmouth in 2023.

He has now become a cult hero at Fratton Park, and he is the club's top scorer in the Championship this season.

His winner in Belfast was a fitting moment for a player who continues to grow on the international stage.

"He's a very valuable player for Portsmouth and I think he's in the process of signing a new contract there, and I imagine a lot of teams in the Championship will be disappointed by that."

While Devlin will get the headlines after his man-of-the-match performance, goalkeeper Pierce Charles came up with a big moment of his own with a superb reflex save to deny Danylo Sikan in the closing stages.

The 21-year-old has yet to concede in the Nations League campaign, and he has produced several big moments to make it 466 minutes and counting without shipping a goal for Northern Ireland.

In front of him, the trio of Ruairi McConville, Tom Atcheson and Ciaron Brown were again rock solid.

"You don't keep five clean sheets because you're good with the ball at your feet. You keep five clean sheets because you make good decisions," O'Neill said on Charles.

"You make saves when it's needed. He kind of does it without any fuss as well, which I think is really good.

"He doesn't come and cause any issues with the back-three, which is very important for any goalkeeper, and he has a good decision-making process and a good understanding of the game."

Northern Ireland will now head to Hungary with their Nations League destiny in their own hands in what is essentially a Group B2 decider.

They are guaranteed a promotion play-off at the very least, but the goal will be to earn automatic elevation to League A for the first time.

Highlights: Devlin nets first international goal to seal victory

Considering Northern Ireland had just one Nations League win in 16 League B matches before the campaign, back-to-back promotions would be a remarkable achievement.

One down side from the win over Ukraine was the two yellow cards accumulated, one for O'Neill and the other for key striker Jamie Donley.

Both were for reactions to a perceived lack of decisions from French referee Francois Letexier, and both manager and player will now watch the game in Budapest from the stands.

"The referee doesn't like my reaction and there's not much I can do about that," O'Neill said.

"I would assume that I'm going to have to watch the game from the stands, but I'll be able to influence it from there, I'm sure."

On Donley's booking, which came for protesting after Letexier failed to stop play when Trai Hume was bleeding from a cut on his head, O'Neill said it was a "poor yellow".

"I thought Jamie had a very good game for us. He'll be a blow for us," he said.

Terry Devlin started his professional career in the Irish Premiership

But the suspensions will do little to dampen what was another encouraging night at Windsor Park.

Hungary had piled the pressure on Northern Ireland by winning in Georgia earlier on Saturday, and Northern Ireland's response sets up a showdown to top the group on Tuesday.

"We were aware that Hungary had won the game earlier and we're in a great position," O'Neill added.

"It would be great to win the group. It will be a tough, tough game but this is a brilliant game for us. It's a great arena to play in."

Having kept five clean sheets in as many matches, O'Neill is targeting completing the campaign without conceding.

If they can do that, they would not only win promotion but secure a play-off for Euro 2028 as a back-up should their qualifying group not go to plan.

"For a nation of our size, with our players at this stage of their careers, to have a chance to win the group and also to be playing Nations League A is a big achievement.

"I think we would probably be one of the smaller nations to play at Nations League A level since the start of the competition.

"We want to try to achieve that and we have a chance to do that on Tuesday night."

#836. Mauricio Pochettino asked the US to believe in his project. Did he believe in it himself?

The coach’s tenure with the USMNT brought a whiplash of highs and lows. He met some goals but also left many with the impression he never truly bought in

It did not take US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino very long to take his first big swing.

He’d just taken the reins of the program after a disastrous performance at the 2024 Copa América cost his predecessor his job, with the first home World Cup in three decades looming on the horizon. The federation introduced him in New York City, on the 24th floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River. In short order, he was asked about the culture surrounding the program. In his answer, he invoked the four-time World Cup champion US women.

“We need to believe that we can win,” Pochettino said that day in September 2024. “That we can win not only a game: We can win the World Cup.”

It is the type of belief that feels almost alien to observers of the US men, the type of statement that American fans yearn to hear so badly from a coach yet also roll their eyes at. For years, fans of men’s soccer in the US have been desperate to taste glory, and for years they have developed an inferiority complex spurred along not only by results but by international perception. Even in the present day, with American players playing in Europe at the very highest level, the idea that the US could win a men’s World Cup feels borderline preposterous.

That never stopped Pochettino from espousing his belief that the US should believe they could make a miraculous run in 2026 and win the whole thing. It was a mantra he returned to frequently during his time leading the team, publicly and privately, even in the weeks leading up to the tournament. Pochettino even told Donald Trump that the US could win it all, perhaps planting the seeds for an assist turned own-goal down the line.

Belief is something that could attract even the most casual US fans, the type of newcomers whose previous experience with an American soccer coach came from Apple TV. Unfortunately for US fans, Pochettino’s actions never quite lined up with the inspirational speech.

There was the near-constant stream of rumors attaching Pochettino to clubs in England, rumors he never really went out of his way to quash even before they tied him to the Manchester United job he has now accepted. In many ways this type of thing is unavoidable and understandable: bringing on a high-profile coach and expecting peace and quiet is the footballing equivalent of dating a supermodel and expecting no one else to make an advance. Yet too often it felt as if Pochettino was the one stoking the fire; it was not uncommon to wake up in the States and find social media feeds populated with clips of the Argentinian espousing the valor of the Premier League and even floating the idea of returning someday.

This was never really shocking or unexpected and was far from offensive. Professional sports are fickle and players, coaches and administrators alike are wise to keep their options open and their bridges intact. Yet it was a bit galling to hear from someone brought in to galvanize the US’s players and fans ahead of a generational event: a home World Cup.

Pochettino also seemed sometimes frustrated by the very thing he was in part brought in to help change: American soccer’s sometimes awkward place in America itself. After losing the 2025 Gold Cup final to Mexico in Houston, he went out of his way to criticize the idea that the US would play in front of a pro-Mexico crowd on home soil, an issue that predates Pochettino by decades and may well never be solved, one even the most cursory research would’ve revealed prior to arrival. He fairly criticized the lack of stakes in Major League Soccer and suggested that US players are coddled throughout their youth development while at the same time butting heads with media who dared question the effects of a group-stage loss to Turkey at this summer’s World Cup. In reality, he faced far less pressure as the head coach of the USMNT than he would have in most any other major footballing nation.

All of it too often gave observers the feeling that Pochettino was never truly bought in. But then, there was the whiplash, which was palpable. As soon as one began to feel that way, there’d be a fresh injection of dopamine – the US’s 4-1 demolishing of Paraguay, for example, far and away their best-ever performance at a World Cup. And there was Poch, nearly in tears and belting out Country Roads, then speaking glowingly about America, American football and everything else that comes along with it. A few weeks later, they’d suffer a 4-1 drubbing at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 that will go down as among the worst-ever performances by the US at a World Cup. Certainly the most traumatic.

Athletes and coaches hate being asked about their legacies, in general. The question in and of itself sounds moribund, as if the person asked is about to ascend into the ether. Legacies, too, are tricky things – they often take years to materialize, and they’re sometimes just as quickly erased by shifting perceptions or the accomplishments of successors.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Pochettino does not seem to be the kind of person who would mind being asked about his legacy; he actually seems more like one who would already have one in mind before departure. Yet when asked by the Guardian on Friday to define his lasting impact, he struggled to do so at first. “I am not arrogant,” Pochettino replied with a smile and a laugh. “Well, not arrogant enough. I am a little bit arrogant.”

Eventually he relented. Pochettino’s lasting impact, the coach said, was largely down to relationships, to having done things the right way, in his mind.

“The most valuable feeling that we get isn’t one victory, or that we helped in the program,” he said. “It is that relationship in the program – even when you cross the sea, you look and smile because I think you share the values that are very important in life, more important than anything else. That is our principal that we respect always.”

Pochettino has always thought in big, broad, ambitious strokes and has executed those visions over the course of his career with varying degrees of success. In the United States, he arrived with varying goals: ensure a proper showing at a home World Cup, help change the perception of the game to the general public and lay down roots for long-term growth.

In some ways, Pochettino certainly succeeded. In others, he’s left the whole of American soccer wanting. It’s a fitting end for a coach who wanted so many people to believe – yet might never have felt that way himself.

#834. Scientists discover stunning new Amazon fish that may already be endangered

A tiny fish with brilliant orange markings has been discovered in the Brazilian Amazon, but scientists warn that the newly identified species may already be at risk of extinction. Found in a handful of forest pools threatened by human activity, the colorful fish has prompted researchers to call for urgent conservation measures.

The new species, named Laimosemion laranja, belongs to a group of small freshwater fish known as killifish. It measures less than three centimeters in standard length, but its appearance is anything but ordinary. Males have rows of bright orange spots along the front half of their bodies, followed by bold orange chevron patterns near the tail. These vivid markings stand out against their pale gray sides.

The discovery was made during fieldwork in the Rio Cajari drainage in southern Amapá, a state in northern Brazil. The research team included scientists from the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte, Instituto Peixe das Nuvens, Universidade Federal do Pará, and University of West Florida.

A Striking Discovery in the Amazon Rainforest

The researchers were exploring how different freshwater fish in the Rivulidae family have evolved their life cycles and survival strategies across Brazil's diverse environments. During their surveys, they encountered a fish whose unusual coloration immediately stood out.

"We are developing a research project aimed at investigating the evolution of life-history strategies in freshwater fishes of the family Rivulidae across different biomes in Brazil," said lead researcher Yuri Abrantes of the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte. "During our sampling in small rivers locally known as 'igarapés' in the Rio Cajari region, in Amapá State, we found this fish with a very striking coloration, which immediately caught our attention."

Although the fish looked different from known species, its appearance alone was not enough to establish that it was new to science. The team carefully examined its body proportions, counted its scales, and studied features of its skeleton. They compared these characteristics with those of closely related species and analyzed its mitochondrial DNA to determine whether it represented a distinct species.

"It was an unexpected moment," Abrantes recalled. "Initially, what most caught our attention was the impressive coloration of the males and females, which was unlike anything we had previously encountered in the study area. This sparked our admiration and a great deal of curiosity."

Genetic testing ultimately confirmed that the fish was a previously unrecognized species. For the researchers, the finding was particularly meaningful because it highlighted how much remains to be discovered in parts of the Amazon that are both poorly studied and increasingly threatened.

Once the genetic analysis confirmed the fish's distinct identity, he said, "it was something special, as we saw an opportunity to contribute to increasing our knowledge of Amazonian biodiversity and to draw attention to the conservation of areas that are still poorly explored but highly threatened."

Why Scientists Named the New Fish Laranja

The name Laimosemion laranja reflects both the fish's remarkable appearance and the place where it was discovered. In Portuguese, laranja means orange, referring to both the color and the fruit. The name also pays tribute to Laranjal do Jari, the municipality in Amapá where the species was found.

"We wanted to choose a name that would highlight a characteristic of the fish while also fostering a sense of connection with the people of the region where it was discovered," Abrantes explained.

Beyond its colorful appearance, the discovery could help scientists better understand the evolution of Amazonian killifish. Some members of this group have developed an extraordinary way to survive in habitats that periodically dry out. Their embryos can stop developing and remain dormant in damp mud, resuming development when seasonal rains refill the pools.

"Laimosemion represents one of the five independent origins of the annual life cycle within the family Rivulidae," said Abrantes. "Laimosemion laranja is particularly interesting because it expands our knowledge of the diversity and evolution of this group in the region."

Newly Discovered Amazon Fish May Already Be Endangered

Despite the excitement surrounding the discovery, the future of Laimosemion laranja is uncertain. Scientists have found it in only three small forest pools near Laranjal do Jari, and every known location shows signs of environmental disturbance.

Deforestation, mining, and urban development are putting pressure on the surrounding habitats. One of the pools is close to water that has been discolored by sediment from mining activities. Another is located within the city itself, where plastic pollution is affecting the environment.

The species' entire known range is estimated to cover just 25 square kilometers. Because its habitat is so restricted and faces multiple threats, the researchers believe the fish meets the criteria for classification as Endangered under guidelines established by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

To improve its chances of survival, the team has recommended expanding the boundaries of the nearby Rio Cajari Extractive Reserve to include the areas where the fish lives.

The discovery adds another species to the Amazon's remarkable biological diversity while underscoring the need to protect habitats that scientists have barely begun to explore. Without stronger conservation measures, species such as Laimosemion laranja could face serious threats before researchers have the opportunity to fully understand them.

The study was published in the open access journal Zoosystematics and Evolution.

#833. Raphinha sees red as Brazil stunned by Japan while Argentina’s post-Messi era starts with defeat

Brazil loss in Singapore marred by unruly end to friendly

Argentina beaten 2-1 by Uruguay in Buenos Aires

Raphinha was sent off as Brazil crashed to a 3-2 defeat by Japan in their international friendly in Singapore. The Barcelona captain had been substituted after 71 minutes, but was shown a red card after protesting against Tatsuhiro Sakamoto’s stoppage-time winner on the touchline. The Brazil head coach, Carlo Ancelotti, was also sent off in a fractious ending to the match.

Japan went 2-0 up inside 20 minutes through Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura. Vinícius Júnior reduced the deficit in the 33rd minute and scored again to drag them level on 75 minutes, before Sakamoto’s controversial late winner.

Argentina’s post-Messi era began with a 2-1 defeat at home against Uruguay in Buenos Aires. The loss marked the World Cup finalists’ first match since Lionel Messi’s international retirement in early October.

Leonardo Balerdi opened the scoring with an own goal in the 48th minute, before Maximiliano Araújo doubled Uruguay’s lead in the 53rd minute under their new coach, Diego Forlán. Julián Álvarez pulled one back for the hosts in the 73rd minute.

This clásico rioplatense on Friday also kicked off a new chapter for Argentina under Lionel Scaloni, who extended his contract to 2030 this week.

Messi’s retirement remains a fresh wound for local fans; notably, the La Bombonera stadium fell short of a sellout, a rare departure from the norm. While most supporters in the stands wore the albiceleste jersey with Messi’s No 10, Scaloni chose not to assign the number for the match. The coach explained he has yet to select a successor and as it is not mandatory he prefers to leave the jersey vacant for now.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

On the pitch, Argentina lacked the explosive, incisive spark Messi typically produced in the final third. Neither Nicolás Paz nor Thiago Almada was able to fill that void. Argentina will hope to bounce back against Costa Rica in Córdoba on Tuesday, while Uruguay host the Dominican Republic on the same day.

#832. How Aston Villa are reclaiming their identity

Aston Villa currently sit ninth in the Women's Super League table

A club's true identity always shows in a local derby and Aston Villa hope to impose theirs when they face rivals Birmingham City on Sunday.

Villa have not had a smooth ride of it this season after a winless start led to the sacking of former manager Natalia Arroyo at the end of September.

The Spaniard helped stabilise Villa during her two years in charge but they lacked consistency, and it left some wondering what their identity really was.

Brian Sorensen is the man in charge of changing that on the pitch now, while there are others off it who are transforming Villa behind the scenes.

"Aston Villa is a club of heart. We put a lot into everything we do," managing director Maggie Murphy told BBC Sport.

"I think a lot of people know we try to do everything the right way, the proper way. We're a club that is the heart of 'proper football' in many ways."

So what are Villa doing this season to get in touch with their values?

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Former Everton boss Brian Sorensen is now managing Aston Villa

Sunday's Women's Super League match with Birmingham (14:00 GMT) marks 30 years since the team officially took the Aston Villa name.

Sorensen hoes it will be the perfect opportunity to showcase who Villa are on the pitch.

"There's a lot of history in this club which maybe not many people know. We need to showcase that," said interim manager Sorensen.

"We want to be really hard-working and humble - like the area we are from - and have a clear identity of how we attack and defend.

"It's trying to align all of that, making sure that we are a team that is recognised, that is one the other teams will fear playing against."

They will celebrate this crucial point in their history in the second city derby at Villa Park, and inform fans of a research project they are undertaking this season.

The project is called 'Roots, Rise and Reach' and hopes to uncover periods of the women's team's history that have never been documented before.

They have already found a newspaper report from 1957 detailing a game between an unofficial Aston Villa Ladies team and Birmingham City.

"It's huge piece of work that we're doing just to understand our own heritage and where we've come from," said Murphy.

"We're very aware that our roots go much further [than 1996]. We're going back decades at the moment trying to uncover some of that history.

"I think it's really important to know where we've come from, because that gives us a sense of identity that maybe we don't always have."

Diving into the club's history is one way Villa are hoping to engage fans this season.

They are trying to grow attendances as part of the club's five-year strategy and last season set up fan forums for the first time.

In response to feedback, they have changed age categories on their ticketing, introduced hospitality season tickets and hosted podcasts with former players and comedians to improve matchday experiences.

They have also been advertising upcoming games on 'digi-vans' throughout the country in the hope of attracting neutral women's football fans.

"There are plenty of floating fans in women's football so we are trying to grab as many as we can and make sure they have the best possible day," added Murphy.

"They might not support Villa the first time they come, but they might after three, four games and buy themselves a claret and blue scarf.

"That's our drive. We want to build this club sustainably and generate the funds that can then go into the football side of the business."

Villa players are happy stop to sign autographs and take photos after games

All of these efforts are part of a wider club ambition to be sustainable and ultimately deliver success on the pitch.

Murphy's task is to make the women's team financially stable, drive revenue and improve atmosphere at games.

She works in tandem with Marisa Ewers, director of women's football, who oversees recruitment, contract renewals and football staff management.

"We want it to be super coherent across both sides. In a really crude way, my job is to make money and Marissa's job is to spend it," said Murphy.

"Our teams work really closely together. Last year, we only had two people in the club that were 100% dedicated to the women's business side. Today, we have nine.

"We are investing in revenue-generating areas. I definitely want us to be competing at the highest possible level consistently, but with heart.

"We want to feel like we have contributed to the story of women's football in this country."

Villa's season is starting to look up. They currently sit ninth with two wins and four draws from their opening nine matches.

They drew with Arsenal at the start of this month after beating Birmingham City in a penalty shootout in their Women's League Cup tie.

With successive matches against newly promoted sides Birmingham and Charlton coming up, can Villa take a step closer to where they want to be?

"Where we are today is born of the hard work of lots of people that have come before us. We need to recognise that and start to steady the ship," said Murphy.

"Villa has not been in the WSL for that long. People forget that. We're still in a very transitional phase - as is the wider women's football ecosystem."

#831. Taylor Frankie Paul's Ex Dakota Mortensen Suing Hulu for Defamation

Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Dakota Mortensen, who has appeared on the Hulu reality show alongside his ex Taylor Frankie Paul, has filed a lawsuit against the network, alleging staged events.

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives alum—who has appeared on the Hulu reality series with his now-ex Taylor Frankie Paul—has filed a lawsuit against the network, as well as Jeff Jenkins Productions and Ludwig Productions, according to court documents obtained by multiple outlets Nov. 13.

In his suit, the 33-year-old alleged that seasons three, four, and five of the series presented him "to millions of viewers as a domestic abuser," per court documents obtained by local outlet ABC4 Utah, "as a man who retaliated against the mother of his child by reporting her to Child Protective Services, and as a serial adulterer.”

Earlier this year, a legal battle between Mortensen and Paul—who share a 2-year-old son—began after he filed to request a protective order against on her on the same day that TMZ published a video of a 2023 physical altercation featuring the former couple.

In April, Paul—who is also mom to two kids with ex-husband Tate Paul—then requested her own temporary restraining order, alleging Mortensen had a "pattern of abusive conduct and coercive control" throughout their on-again, off-again romance.

Later that month, per Today, a judge granted mutual protective orders.

Mortensen also alleges in his lawsuit against the network that producers created storylines "assembled from staged events and from the deliberate deletion of footage that contradicted the storyline, and published after the producers had been informed by Mortensen and by others, that the allegations were false."

More specifically, Mortensen alleges cameras captured Paul striking Mortensen with a pizza box while filming season five, per ABC 4 Utah, and demanded that the footage be included in the episodes that aired, but that it was excluded from the final cut.

E! News has reached out to Paul’s reps for comment about the alleged incident.

“The knowingly false portrayal of Mortensen as the abuser in the relationship continued uninterrupted," the suit states, "while the only footage of physical aggression between the two, aggression by Paul against Mortensen, was intentionally withheld from viewers to promote a false narrative."

Mortensen is asking for compensatory damages, ABC 4 Utah reports, as well as other damages. E! News has reached out to Hulu and Mortensen's attorney for comment and has not yet heard back.

In mid-April, Paul was granted supervised visitation with her and Mortensen's son and one week later, the Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office announced in a news release it would not be filing charges against her after completing two separate investigations led by the Draper Police Department and West Jordan Police Department.

For his part, Mortensen previously described the situation between the two as “deeply upsetting.”

“I am focusing on our son and his safety,” he told E! News in a statement in March, “and hope that Taylor will do the same.”

For a closer look at the timeline of the allegations made between Paul and Mortensen, keep reading…

Feb. 17, 2023: Taylor Frankie Paul Arrested Following Confrontation With Dakota Mortensen

After rising to fame with #MomTok, Taylor Frankie Paul was arrested in Utah on Feb. 17, 2023 stemming from an incident with then boyfriend Dakota Mortensen. She was accused of throwing metal chairs and a wooden playset at him while one of her two children—who she shares with ex-husband Tate Paul—was in the room, per an affidavit obtained by ABC 4 Utah.

Paul was charged with one count of felony aggravated assault, two counts of felony domestic violence in the presence of a child causing injury, one count of misdemeanor child abuse and one count of misdemeanor criminal mischief, according to court documents released by the District Attorney for Salt Lake County and obtained by E! News at the time.

A Herriman Police Department officer who responded to the incident said that when he arrived, Mortensen "reported he was in an argument with his girlfriend,” according to a written declaration in the court documents. The officer further stated that "during the argument, Mortensen attempted to leave the residence, however [Paul] began hitting him."

August 2023: Taylor Frankie Paul Pleads Guilty to Aggravated Assault

Paul pleaded guilty to a third-degree felony count of aggravated assault in August 2023, according to court documents obtained by the Salt Lake Tribune, while four other charges were dismissed with prejudice.

Her plea was held in abeyance for three years, at which time the charge would be entered as a Class A misdemeanor as long as Paul abided by the terms of her plea agreement, per the documents.

According to her plea deal, Paul was to obtain both a substance abuse evaluation and a domestic violence evaluation and complete any recommended treatment over a three-year period—as well as not violate any major laws.

March 19, 2024: Taylor Frankie Paul and Dakota Mortensen Welcome Son

Paul and Mortensen's son was born a week early, with Paul posting a photo from the hospital to Instagram on April 4, 2024 and writing, “We’ve had the best two weeks with him. We all love you so much, thank you for blending our family.”

September 2024: Taylor Frankie Paul Speaks Out About 2023 Arrest

Paul admitted in an interview with E! News that the altercation with Mortensen was their “rock bottom for sure.”

"He stood by me with that because he knew everything going on behind closed doors,” she said. “That was a horrible night and I'm full of regret. Dakota has been at rock bottom himself, so he could totally relate. He was like, 'I want to help you out of this.'"

As for the confrontation itself, she later said the incident had been building up.

“I had an ectopic [pregnancy] a few months prior, and then I had a chemical pregnancy,” she shared on the Viall Files podcast in September 2024. “I don't want to blame hormones, but I will put that into account. Like, I am pretty whack.”

Paul added that the events had left her feeling lost and angry, saying, "I was feeling so low I went and drank that night. And Dakota picks me up and he’s angry that I drank."

"I remember throwing things, and I don't know my daughters on the couch. We had babysitters there, so I think they’re upstairs sleeping," she said, alleging that Mortensen tried to tell her that her then 5-year-old daughter was present, but "I'm like so gone I don’t care, and I throw another chair."

Sept. 6, 2024: Secret Lives of Mormon Wives Premieres

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives debuted on Hulu in September 2024, with the first episode of season one featuring Paul's 2023 arrest.

May 18, 2025: Taylor Frankie Paul Confirms Dakota Mortensen Breakup After On-Again, Off-Again Relationship

Paul confirmed their split in May 2025 after it was revealed on the season two premiere of SLOMW that Mortensen had cheated on her shortly after they had welcomed their son, writing on TikTok, "Dakota isn’t mine anymore, wish him the best.”

"Dakota and I were living together and in bliss with our new baby, and I was even considering engagement,” she said on the premiere episode. “And then I learned that he was lying this entire time.”

During a season four episode of SLOMW, Mortensen admitted to cheating with their friend Shinia Powell, telling Taylor during a FaceTime call, “Was it dumb of me? Yes. Could I have picked someone else? Yes. Who it was matters, and that's where I think I went wrong. I picked somebody that was obviously going to come with problems, and that was very s--tty of me to do."

Sept. 10, 2025: Taylor Frankie Paul Is Cast as The Bachelorette for Season 22

In a surprising turn of events, Paul was cast as the leading lady for season 22 of The Bachelorette, confirming the news during an appearance on Call Her Daddy in September 2025. The decision marked a notable departure for the franchise, as it usually casts suitors from previous seasons of The Bachelor in the position.

But for Paul, it was a welcome change, saying in a teaser for the season, “I do believe I was gifted this for another chapter in my life.”

“I’ve been criticized, I’ve been judged and I’ve been rejected,” Paul continued, “but anyone that takes the time to know me will see that I’m actually a genuine person and I mean well and a person that deserves another chance at love.”

Fall 2025: Taylor Frankie Paul and Dakota Mortensen FaceTime Before Filming Begins on The Bachelorette

Shortly before Paul began filming season 22 of The Bachelorette, she and Mortensen shared an emotional conversation seen during a season four episode of SLOMW, during which he apologized for having a relationship with Shinia, saying it was "very s--tty of me to do."

He added that he and Paul had both done “a lot of things” to “hurt each other,” but believed that overall the two still loved each other.

The pair agreed their relationship was “toxic,” with Paul saying that being on The Bachelorette "will be one the best things for us, regardless of what happens. This would be the best break and breakoff of our cycle. You could do a lot of healing."

But Mortensen made it clear he was still interested in a relationship, telling Paul, “I'm happy for you. I want you to be happy. That's what I'm saying, if you find someone, like, great. But all I'm gonna say—save a rose for me, 'kay?"

February 2026: Taylor Frankie Paul and Dakota Mortensen's Domestic Assault Investigation Opened

Filming for season five of Secret Lives of Mormon Wives was put on hold after an alleged confrontation between Paul and Mortensen in February 2026.

A spokesperson for the Draper City Police Department confirmed to People on March 16 that there was an open "domestic assault investigation" regarding Paul and Mortensen—telling the outlet that "allegations have been made in both directions.” The spokesperson explained "contact was made with involved parties on [Feb] 24th and 25th,” but declined to share more information due to the ongoing investigation.

As a source shared with E! News, "Taylor owns her mistakes, all she wants to do is protect her son, Ever, from stories in the press or anything negative about his father and wants him to think well of his father."

March 19, 2026: Footage From Taylor Frankie Paul and Dakota Mortensen’s 2023 Confrontation Surfaces

Following news of Paul and Mortensen's 2026 dispute, video footage from their physical altercation in 2023 was released by TMZ.

In the video, Mortensen can be seen recording the fight on his phone as Paul yells at him and attempts to strike him, at one point putting him in a headlock.

"Look," Mortensen can be heard saying, "this is called physical abuse."

He could also be heard telling her that her daughter was present as Paul began throwing metal barstools at him. During the altercation, Paul accused Mortensen of pushing her to the floor before he started recording, while he alleged, "You did this," and asked her to help her then-5-year-old. Later, Paul could be heard yelling, "Get away from my daughter."

The responding police officer’s written declaration obtained by E! News in 2023 confirmed the child was hit by one of the stools.

After the video was published, a spokesperson for Paul told E! News in a statement that the video was part of "a destructive campaign to harm" her, saying it "conveniently omits context" and was meant to "distract" from Mortensen's actions. As for the real estate agent, he denied her claims as "baseless."

March 19, 2026: ABC Cancels Taylor Frankie Paul’s Season of The Bachelorette

After video of the 2023 altercation between Paul and Mortensen surfaced, ABC confirmed that it would be cancelling season 22 of The Bachelorette, with a spokesperson for Disney Entertainment saying in a statement to E! News, “We have made the decision to not move forward with the new season of The Bachelorette at this time, and our focus is on supporting the family.”

March 19, 2026: Taylor Frankie Paul Speaks Out on Bachelorette Cancelation

Following ABC’s decision, Paul broke her silence about the situation.

"Taylor is very grateful for ABC’s support as she prioritizes her family’s safety and security," her rep told E! News. "After years of silently suffering extensive mental and physical abuse as well as threats of retaliation, Taylor is finally gaining the strength to face her accuser and taking steps to ensure that she and her children are protected from any further harm."

The statement continued, "There are too many women who are suffering in silence as they survive aggressive, jealous ex-partners who refuse to let them move on with their lives."

Her rep confirmed that Paul was "currently exploring all of her options, seeking support, and preparing to own and share her story."

March 19, 2026: Dakota Mortensen Breaks Silence on the Allegations

Mortensen spoke out about the domestic violence allegations between himself and Paul, telling E! News in a March 19 statement, "As anyone who has seen the video will understand, this is a deeply upsetting situation."

"I am, unfortunately, used to these baseless claims about me and our relationship," he said, "which I categorically deny."

"I am focusing on our son and his safety," Paul added, "and hope that Taylor will do the same."

March 20, 2026: Dakota Mortensen Granted Temporary Custody of Son

Mortensen was awarded temporary custody of their son after filing for a protective order against Paul, according to documents obtained by People March 20. A hearing in the matter was scheduled for April 7—where Taylor would be allowed to speak and share her side—but until then, the order stated that "no parent time is allowed," per the outlet.

March 24, 2026: Third Police Investigation

Authorities in Utah began investigating another alleged domestic violence incident that took place in 2024 which Mortensen brought to the police's attention in February, a West Jordan Police Department spokesperson told NBC News March 24. While investigators spoke to Paul's attorney, they had not yet spoken to her directly, and hoped for her to submit a written statement or be interviewed to corroborate details of Mortensen's report, per the spokesperson.

April 14, 2026: Salt Lake County District Attorney's Office Announced It Would Not File New Charges Against Taylor Frankie Paul

A week after Paul was granted supervised visitation with her and Mortensen's son during an April 7 court hearing, The Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office announced in a news release it would not be filing charges against her after two separate investigations led by the Draper Police Department and West Jordan Police Department, according to the Salt Lake Tribune.

According to the outlet, the news release noted, "Due to the high profile of the defendant, the cases were reviewed by multiple attorneys."

#830. Chelsea go top of WSL as Sandy Baltimore bullet sees off Manchester City

Pragmatic, resolute and gutsy. Sonia Bompastor showed her ruthless side and delivered a tactical masterclass as Chelsea earned a 1-0 win over Manchester City and leapfrogged them at the top of the Women’s Super League.

Lucy Bronze credited fellow full-back Katie McCabe with firing Chelsea up pre-match, having told them they “had to be dogs” in the game, and a dogged performance followed. Sandy Baltimore’s stunning strike in added time at the end of the first half was the difference as the west London side nullified the threat of a team that had scored in each of their preceding 21 games in all competitions, inflicting their first loss of the campaign.

The task for City got even tougher when goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita received a straight red for clattering into Alyssa Thompson, but despite their numerical disadvantage it was end to end right up until the final whistle.

“It always affects you when you go one player down,” said manager Andrée Jeglertz. “But we handled that and that’s not why we lose the game. I think it’s small details. It’s a tight game, it’s two great football teams, there’s a lot of situations, there’s a lot of battles and they managed to score on their big chance from a great finish. We also have a couple of great opportunities where we don’t manage to score.”

Momentum was with City going into the match after their 5-0 defeat of West Ham the preceding weekend and a 4-1 win against Inter in the Champions League on Tuesday night and they were able to welcome the injured duo Vivianne Miedema and Beth Mead back to the bench to bolster their matchday squad.

At Stamford Bridge the England women’s manager, Sarina Wiegman, the US women’s manager, Emma Hayes, and passionate women’s football advocate and pundit Ian Wright were in the stands. It was a fixture that promised much, and it delivered: the league’s most potent attacks, with Chelsea having scored 28 league goals before this fixture to City’s 27, while Bompastor’s side had the most solid defence, having conceded only five times before kick-off.

Manchester United captain Maya le Tissier marked her 150th appearance for the club with a superb strike in a 2-0 victory over Crystal Palace at the Progress with Unity Stadium. Presented with a framed shirt before kick-off, Le Tissier whipped a low shot from distance into the net in the 18th minute before Elisabeth Terland confirmed United’s win after the hour mark.

United moved up to fourth with the win and they kept hold of the position after Tottenham drew a blank in a goalless draw at home to Everton, whose winless run in the league stretched to five matches. In the day’s late game, Liverpool ended a five-match winless run in the WSL by easing past Brighton 3-0. Press Association

It was a chess match. After a thrillingly frenetic start there was a change for Chelsea just 12 minutes in, with the centre-back Kadeisha Buchanan replaced by Veerle Buurman. There was speculation over whether the withdrawal of the Canadian defender was due to injury and Bompastor unconvincingly claimed it was.

“Yesterday in training, she got a knock to her head during contact with a teammate. She was fine after the training session. She was fine in the evening. We assessed her again this morning and everything was fine,” she said. “I just felt watching her from the beginning of the game, she was not herself. Then I took the responsibility to make the substitution. But for me, I was almost forced to do that because I know my player and I know she was not in the game.”

However, if, as many believe, the defensive switch was a tactical decision, it was a stroke of genius, as Buurman was excellent at nullifying the threat of Khadija Shaw.

“She had a really good performance against a top player,” said Bompastor. “Today was positive. But again, as I’ve told you previously, when it doesn’t work it’s not so positive.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

There were chances at both ends but they were limited and it took until the fourth of five added minutes for Chelsea to draw first blood. The goal was sensational. Baltimore collected the ball just inside the box on the right, from Ellie Carpenter, lined up her shot and sent a piledriver of a strike into the roof of the net.

It was the only shot on target in the first half.

City sought an instant reply after the break but they could not find a way through and momentum ebbed and flowed. Jeglertz withdrew Sam Coffey and Mary Fowler in favour of Miedema and Laura Blindkilde Brown to help his side assert some authority in the middle and, through Miedema, to add some creative instinct.

However, as City pushed they left themselves vulnerable on the break and when Maika Hamano’s crossfield ball was met by Alyssa Thompson with just over 15 minutes remaining it was disaster for City. Yamashita raced out of her box and clattered into the Chelsea forward, conceding a free-kick and receiving a straight red card.

Despite City’s efforts, Chelsea were in control and they held strong to blow the title race wide open.
